where: Section 2 (n = 0 bullet), worked example step 1, parity sentence in Section 2
problem: Powers are not marked up in several prose formulas, so they read as products. The n = 0 bullet shows "P0(x) = 1/(20·0!) d0/dx0[(x²−1)0]", which literally reads 1 divided by 20·0! = 1/20, not 1. Similarly "2nn!", "dn/dxn", "(−x) = (−1)nPn(x)" and the definition line "2n = 2 multiplied n times" read as 2·n, not 2 to the power n. Unicode superscripts are used correctly elsewhere (2², 2³), so the chapter is inconsistent and a student can misread the formula.
fix: Use <sup> everywhere: P<sub>0</sub>(x) = 1/(2<sup>0</sup>·0!) d<sup>0</sup>/dx<sup>0</sup>[(x²−1)<sup>0</sup>] = 1; P<sub>n</sub>(x) = (1/(2<sup>n</sup> n!)) d<sup>n</sup>/dx<sup>n</sup>[(x²−1)<sup>n</sup>]; P<sub>n</sub>(−x) = (−1)<sup>n</sup>P<sub>n</sub>(x); and rewrite the definition as "2<sup>n</sup> means 2 multiplied by itself n times".

where: Section 1, last two bullets, and Quiz Q2 answer
problem: The test for a regular singular point is stated as if a simple zero of the coefficient of y″ were enough by itself. That is only true when the other two coefficients are analytic at the point. Here the coefficient of y′ is −2x and the coefficient of y is n(n+1), both analytic everywhere, so the conclusion is right but the reasoning as written is incomplete.
fix: Say: "At x = ±1 the coefficient of y″ is 1−x², which has a simple zero, while −2x and n(n+1) are analytic there; a simple zero of the y″ coefficient with the other two coefficients analytic makes the point a regular singular point. So x = ±1 are regular singular points."

problem: The chapter calls this a Sturm-Liouville equation with weight 1 on [−1, 1] but does not say that the problem is singular, because p(x) = 1−x² vanishes at both ends. Without that, a student cannot see why the usual Sturm-Liouville boundary conditions are replaced by keeping y finite at x = ±1, and why only n = 0, 1, 2, … gives an acceptable polynomial solution.
fix: Add one sentence: "Here p(x) = 1−x² is zero at both ends, so this is a singular Sturm-Liouville problem; the boundary condition is that y stays finite at x = ±1, and only n = 0, 1, 2, … satisfies it with a polynomial."
